title: Nvidia Stock Is Down 12% From Its High. Here's What History Says Happens Next.
detail:
Nvidia Stock Is Down 12% From Its High. Here's What History Says Happens Next.
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Tue, October 27, 2026 at 1:01 PM MST 4 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has had a rough few weeks. While it notched a new all-time high at the start of October, the stock has sold off and is now down over 10% from that level. That's a notable sell-off, especially given that it's the world's largest company by market cap.

But is it the perfect buying opportunity right now? Let's take a look at what history says to find out.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Sizable drops are nothing new for Nvidia

Nvidia may have been available to invest in for nearly three decades, but its current business state has only been relevant since 2023, when the AI arms race began. If you look at a stock chart that uses the starting price of 2023 as the high point for Nvidia and then look at drops after that, you can see that selling off 10% or more is nothing new.

NVDA data by YCharts

In fact, it appears that Nvidia spends about as much time 10% or more off its all-time high as it does near its all-time high. So, this is familiar territory for Nvidia investors. The question is, is it a buy now?

I think the best way to assess this is to look at Nvidia's valuation. The best way to assess Nvidia's stock is the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, which uses analyst estimates to determine what its earnings over this fiscal year will be. From this perspective, Nvidia is extremely cheap, but there's one glaring thing that hasn't happened yet.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts

Normally, Nvidia's stock rallies to a 40-times forward earnings level by year-end. It hasn't done that this year, and if it did, that would roughly result in the stock doubling.

I doubt that happens, but the market is essentially not pricing in any 2027 growth, which is a huge oversight. Nvidia has already announced to investors that it expects to deliver nearly 90% year-over-year revenue growth for the upcoming quarter. This is far greater than many big tech stocks and will likely lead to a strong stock performance next year. None of this seems to be priced in because Nvidia trades at such a low forward P/E ratio.

To put its 22.7 times forward earnings price tag in perspective, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) trades for 19.2 times forward earnings. That means Nvidia is barely getting a premium over the broader market despite telling investors it will nearly double revenue in the next quarter. That's a huge arbitrage opportunity, and investors should use this sell-off to scoop up shares.

title: PayPal Just Raised Its Profit Forecast, and the Stock Barely Moved. Here’s Why
detail:
PayPal Just Raised Its Profit Forecast, and the Stock Barely Moved. Here’s Why
Matt Frankel, CFP®, The Motley Fool
Tue, October 27, 2026 at 1:06 PM MST 4 min read
PYPL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

At first glance, PayPal's (NASDAQ:PYPL) third-quarter results looked rather strong. Adjusted EPS grew by 8% year-over-year and handily beat analyst estimates, and management raised its full-year profit guidance.

However, the stock initially fell modestly after the earnings report, and as of 2 p.m. ET on earnings day, it was higher by just 1%, despite the impressive earnings beat and guidance raise. Here's what is worrying investors, and why a beat and raise isn't enough to move the stock higher.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: PayPal.

Here's what disappointed investors

In the third quarter, PayPal's revenue grew by just 2% to $8.58 billion, which fell short of expectations. Transaction margin dollars, a gross profit indicator, rose by only 2%.

The bigger issue is branded checkout. This is the PayPal button you can click on when shopping online. It's PayPal's most profitable business, but payment volume grew by just 1% on a currency-neutral basis. That is the fourth consecutive quarter that we've seen branded checkout growth in the 1% to 2% range. The company's transaction take rate, which is the share of each dollar it keeps as revenue, declined to 1.58% from 1.64% a year earlier, and management is only forecasting slight growth in transaction margin dollars for the fourth quarter.

What is going well

To be fair, several parts of PayPal's business are performing quite well. Venmo is a standout, with payment volume growing 14% year over year. Buy now, pay later (BNPL) volume grew 25%. And payment volume on PayPal and Venmo debit cards in the United States grew by more than 60%.

These are all becoming significant growth engines for the business, and management expects financial services products like these to make up more than 20% of transaction margin dollars this year. But that still leaves 80% of transaction margin dollars coming from low-growth revenue streams.

The real source of PayPal's earnings growth

PayPal grew its earnings per share by 8%, despite growing gross profit by just 2%. How did this happen? The answer is that cost reductions and buybacks are the primary drivers of earnings growth. The company has eliminated over 2,000 roles and is targeting over $1.5 billion in annual savings over the next few years, and PayPal has spent $6 billion buying back its own stock over the past 12 months, reducing its weighted share count by 11%.

title: What a $10,000 Investment in SpaceX Could Be Worth by the End of 2027 After Elon Musk's Shocking Revenue Guidance
detail:
What a $10,000 Investment in SpaceX Could Be Worth by the End of 2027 After Elon Musk's Shocking Revenue Guidance
Geoffrey Seiler, The Motley Fool
Tue, October 27, 2026 at 1:03 PM MST 6 min read
SPCX
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

With about $10,000, investors could buy 70 shares of SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) now, and the stock could more than double over the next year.

CEO Elon Musk shocked many investors on SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call when he projected the company could end 2027 with annual recurring revenue (ARR) of between $500 billion and $1 trillion. Ahead of the quarterly report, analysts were projecting that the space company would generate revenue of $132.4 billion in 2027 and $249.4 billion in 2028. While ARR and revenue are quite different metrics -- ARR is more akin to a year-end revenue run rate -- the clear implication is that Musk thinks SpaceX can blow away Wall Street's revenue consensus.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

After the Oct. 20 report, analysts naturally were scrambling to raise their revenue targets. This includes Brian Gesuale of Raymond James, who roughly doubles his revenue estimates for SpaceX through 2028, while keeping a market-high $800 price target on the stock. The consensus for SpaceX revenue is now up to $180.6 billion for 2027 and $330.9 billion for 2028. That's still a far cry from what Musk's forecast would imply, although that average is likely to drift higher as more analysts make upward revisions.

How SpaceX gets to more than $500 billion in ARR in 2027

There are a few ways for SpaceX to get over $500 billion in ARR by the end of 2027 as a stand-alone company. The biggest driver of revenue growth is going to be leasing out AI infrastructure. Because SpaceX is using short-term leases for data center capacity, it currently commands strong pricing power in a compute-starved world. From the point that capacity comes online and gets leased, SpaceX expects to recoup its upfront investments in that capacity in about a year. Given the rapid pace at which it expects to start turning a profit on those investments, we can expect the company to aggressively increase its capex to build out additional compute capacity.

In its second-quarter report, SpaceX forecast that it would end the year with 2 gigawatts of computing power; three months later, Musk said that it could end 2026 with up to 3 gigawatts. However, the biggest change in his forecast was for 2027. On the company's Q2 call, Musk said SpaceX would likely end 2027 with cumulative compute capacity closer to 10 gigawatts than 5 gigawatts. On the Q3 earnings call, though, he predicted SpaceX would end 2027 with around 13 gigawatts of compute capacity, with a long-shot goal of adding a massive 20 gigawatts of incremental computing power next year.
